opus-5.5.text:
I think it's mostly because, if I look back at almost everything I've worked on, the common thread has always been the same question: how do we learn good representations of the world? Whether it was the early work on network architectures like ResNeXt, or self-supervised learning, or more recently things connected to generative models and multimodal systems, underneath it all I've really been asking what makes a representation useful, and how a model can come to understand visual data rather than just fit labels.

And I like the label because it's not tied to a particular method or trend. Architectures change, training paradigms change. A few years ago everyone was doing supervised pretraining on ImageNet, then contrastive learning, then masked modeling, and now diffusion and large language models are everywhere. But the core problem of representation doesn't go away. Even in generative modeling, I increasingly feel that the quality of the internal representation is what really determines how well the model works, and that's something we've tried to show in some of our recent work.

There's also a slightly more personal reason. I think representation learning is close to the essence of intelligence. If you want a system that can perceive, reason, and act in the real world, it has to build some internal model of that world, a compact, structured way of encoding what it sees. Language models have shown how powerful that can be for text, but I still believe vision and the physical world are a big frontier where we haven't figured out the right representations yet. So calling myself someone who does representation learning is a way of saying that's the problem I care about, regardless of which tools happen to be popular at the moment.

r002.rationale: The candidate says the label is not tied to a method or trend and that representation remains the core problem as architectures and training paradigms change, conveying an enduring research identity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's because, if you look at everything I've worked on over the years, there's actually one thread running through all of it. ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, self-supervised learning with MAE and the data-augmentation work, and more recently generative models like DiT and REPA. On the surface those look like very different projects. Architecture design, generative modeling, pretraining. But the question I'm actually asking is the same every time: how does a model learn a good internal representation of the world, and what does "good" even mean?

For me the architecture was never the goal in itself. ConvNeXt wasn't about convolutions beating transformers. It was about understanding what inductive biases actually matter for learning useful features from visual data. The same with diffusion. When we did REPA, the surprising thing was that a generative model trains much faster and better if you align its internal features to a strong pretrained visual encoder. That tells you the generative model is secretly trying to learn a representation, and it struggles to do that on its own.

So I say "representation learning" because it's the honest description of what I care about. The models, the losses, the data pipelines, those all change every two years. The question of what a model understands about an image, and how we get it to understand more, doesn't change. That's the thing I keep coming back to.

r001.rationale: The response describes learning useful internal representations, but does not define it as mapping data into a space whose properties support downstream tasks.

r002.rationale: It presents representation learning as the consistent question behind projects and models that change over time, describing it as the enduring focus of Xie’s research.

astra-6.text:
I think representation learning is the common thread through the problems I’ve worked on. In computer vision, you start with pixels, but pixels aren’t necessarily the most useful way to describe what’s in an image. The question is: how do you learn a representation that captures the structure and meaning, so that a model can use it to recognize objects, understand a scene, or do something else?

What interests me is how that representation emerges—how it’s shaped by the architecture, the data, and the learning objective. Supervised learning and self-supervised learning are different ways of approaching that question. So I describe myself as working on representation learning because it captures the underlying interest, rather than tying me to one particular task or method.

r001.rationale: The response says a useful representation captures image structure and meaning for tasks such as recognition, but does not define it as mapping data into a space.

r002.rationale: The response calls representation learning an underlying interest across tasks and methods, but does not connect that identity to the field’s rapid evolution.

sol-6.1.text:
I think representation learning is the thread connecting a lot of the problems I’m interested in. When we work with images or videos, the raw input is just pixels. The question is: how do we turn those pixels into something useful—something that captures the structure of the world and helps a model understand what’s happening?

You can approach that through different architectures, different training objectives, or different kinds of supervision. Those things change, but the underlying question stays the same: what should the model learn to represent, and how do we get it to learn that? So I find representation learning a broader and more useful description of my interests than any particular task or method.

r001.rationale: The response says pixels are turned into something useful that captures structure and helps a model understand, but it does not clearly define a mapping into a representational space or say that the space facilitates downstream tasks.

r002.rationale: It says architectures, objectives, and supervision change while the underlying question stays the same, making representation learning a broader identity than any particular task or method.
